288.title: The small holocaust, 1746
288.hook: thousands of Sikhs are killed in a campaign near Kahnuwan
288.tomorrow: The Dal Khalsa and the council
288.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Chhota Ghallughara of 1746 in their histories and at gurdwaras, and the martyrs of the eighteenth century are named in general terms in Ardas, the daily prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kesh, and your line, he kept his kesh. Did you feed someone far from home? Today is a day of remembering, and it asks us to go gently. Day two hundred eighty-eight.

Some families have a year nobody mentions lightly. The year of the flood, the fire, the war. The older relatives lower their voices when it comes up, and the children learn, without being told, that this is something you remember carefully. The Sikh community has two years like that in the eighteenth century, and they have names. The first came in 1746, in the marshes and hills of northern Punjab. Today: Chhota Ghallughara, the small holocaust.
screen: `A YEAR FAMILIES REMEMBER CAREFULLY.` → `TWO SUCH YEARS, WITH NAMES.` → `THE FIRST: 1746.`

segments.voice: Ghallughara is the Punjabi word Sikhs use for a massacre, a great destruction. Chhota means small, only because a larger one would come sixteen years later. In 1746, a senior official in Lahore named Lakhpat Rai lost his brother in a clash with a Sikh band. He swore to wipe out the Sikhs in return. First, Sikhs living in Lahore were rounded up and killed. Then he led a large army, with cannon, to the marshy forest of Kahnuwan, near the Beas and Ravi rivers, where thousands of Sikhs, fighters along with women, children and old people, were camped. The Sikhs fled north toward the hills, hoping for shelter. They were trapped between the soldiers behind them, a swollen river, and hill rulers who wouldn't let them in. Over several weeks in the early summer, thousands were killed, and many who were captured were taken to Lahore and executed. The numbers in the old accounts vary, and are often given as around seven thousand killed and three thousand captured. Nobody knows exactly. Sikhs don't tell this story to stir up hatred. The people who did this are long gone, and no one living today carries the blame. They tell it so the people who died aren't forgotten, and because of what came next. The survivors regrouped. Within a few years they were stronger and better organized than before, as we'll see tomorrow.
screen: `GHALLUGHARA — A GREAT DESTRUCTION.` · `KAHNUWAN, 1746.` · `TRAPPED BETWEEN ARMY, RIVER AND HILLS.` · `REMEMBERED, NOT TURNED TO HATE.` · then, large: `REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is simple. A minute of silence. Sit still, with your hands resting. You don't need to imagine anything, and you don't need to feel anything particular. Just hold a quiet space for people you'll never know, who were lost that summer, and for anyone, anywhere, whose family carries a year like that. If you pray, you can let the silence be your prayer. When the minute passes, keep sitting. The bell holds the time.
Chhota Ghallughara. The small holocaust of 1746, when thousands of Sikhs were killed in a campaign near Kahnuwan. Remembered, not turned to hate.
Your line: remembered. Today, when you hear of someone's loss, near or far, pause for one breath to remember them. Day two hundred eighty-eight.

289.title: The Dal Khalsa and the council
289.hook: Sikh bands unite, meeting at Amritsar and deciding together before the Guru
289.howItsDone: Sikh assemblies still pass gurmatas, resolutions made in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib and sealed with Ardas; the Sarbat Khalsa, a gathering of the whole community at the Akal Takht, is the traditional forum.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Chhota Ghallughara, and your line, remembered. We said the survivors grew stronger. Today, how: they learned to decide together. Day two hundred eighty-nine.

A simple plan can take three days in a group chat. Everyone has an opinion, two people aren't speaking, and in the end nothing happens. Now make the group many independent bands of riders, each with its own leader, its own pride, its own old quarrels. And the stakes aren't dinner plans. They're survival. The Sikhs of the 1740s found a way to make that group decide, and stick to it. It happened twice a year, in Amritsar. Today: gurmata.
screen: `THE GROUP CHAT THAT NEVER DECIDES.` → `MANY PROUD BANDS.` → `TWICE A YEAR, IN AMRITSAR.`

segments.voice: Gurmata joins two words. Gur, the Guru. And mata, a resolution, a considered decision. A gurmata is a decision made in the presence of the Guru, and so binding on everyone. Here's how it worked. Even in the hunted years, the scattered Sikh bands would try to gather at Amritsar at Vaisakhi in spring and Diwali in autumn. The whole assembly was called the Sarbat Khalsa, the entire Khalsa. They met before the Akal Takht, with the Guru Granth Sahib present. Leaders who might be rivals the rest of the year sat down together. Old quarrels were supposed to be left at the door. Matters were discussed openly, and when the assembly reached agreement, it was sealed with Ardas, the prayer. From then on it was a gurmata, not one leader's plan but the Guru's decision, and every band was bound by it. A turning point came at Vaisakhi, 1748. Two years after the small holocaust, the Sarbat Khalsa resolved to bring the many bands together into one army, the Dal Khalsa, the army of the Khalsa, under a single commander, Jassa Singh Ahluwalia. Separate bands, one body. Notice what gave the decision its weight. Not the loudest voice or the biggest band. The presence of the Guru, and the agreement of the whole. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct, still describes how a gurmata is made. There's a small lesson in it for any family or team. A decision people make together, in front of what they all respect, holds better than one someone forces through. And the thing everyone bows to can be bigger than any single person in the room.
screen: `GUR + MATA — A DECISION BEFORE THE GURU.` · `THE SARBAT KHALSA MEETS AT AMRITSAR.` · `RIVALS SIT DOWN TOGETHER.` · `1748: MANY BANDS, ONE DAL KHALSA.` · then, large: `DECIDE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Think of a decision coming up that affects other people: what to cook, where to go, how to split a job, a family plan. Notice whether you were planning to just decide it yourself, or let it drift. Picture instead asking the others, listening properly, and choosing together, with something you all care about in the middle of the table. Pick the decision, and the people you'll ask. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Gurmata. A decision made by the gathered Khalsa in the presence of the Guru, and binding on all. Gur, the Guru, and mata, a resolution.
Your line: decide together. Today, make one decision with the people it affects, instead of for them. Day two hundred eighty-nine.

290.title: Baba Deep Singh, 1757
290.hook: the old scholar-warrior rides to free the Harmandir; tradition says he fought on with his head in his hand
290.howItsDone: Pilgrims at the Harmandir Sahib stop at the place in the parikrama where tradition says Baba Deep Singh fell, and Gurdwara Shaheedan in Amritsar honors him and his companions; his birthday and martyrdom are marked each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurmata, the decision made before the Guru. Your line was decide together. Today, a promise made by one old man, and kept. Day two hundred ninety.

Walk around the pool at the Golden Temple and you'll pass a small shrine where people stop, bow and whisper. Many visitors are surprised by the painting they often see of the man it remembers: an old warrior with a long white beard, sword in one hand, and his own head held in the other. It sounds like a legend. Sikhs tell it with love and awe, and they also tell you why it matters more than the miracle. Today: Baba Deep Singh.
screen: `A SMALL SHRINE BY THE POOL.` → `SWORD IN ONE HAND.` → `HIS HEAD IN THE OTHER.`

segments.voice: Baba means elder, grandfather, a title of love for someone old and wise. Deep Singh was, first of all, a scholar. Tradition says he took amrit from Guru Gobind Singh himself, and spent years at Damdama Sahib, the Guru's seat of learning, copying the Guru Granth Sahib by hand so that more Sikhs could have it. Some of those copies were sent to the takhts. He was also a warrior, and by 1757 an old one, around seventy-five. That year, forces of the Afghan king Ahmad Shah Abdali occupied Amritsar and desecrated the Harmandir. When the news reached Damdama Sahib, Baba Deep Singh made a vow: he would go to Amritsar and free it, or die trying. Riders joined him along the way. Tradition says he drew a line on the ground and asked only those ready to give their lives to cross it. The Afghan army met them a few miles from Amritsar, and the fighting was fierce. Here the accounts differ. The best-known tradition says his head was struck off, and he held it on his palm and kept fighting until he reached the sacred precinct, and laid it there. Other accounts say he was mortally wounded in the neck and fought on to the end. Either way, he finished what he'd vowed. Sikhs find the image powerful because it pictures a promise that outlasts even the body. You don't need a battlefield to feel its pull. Most of us make vows every week, small ones, and leave them half done. Baba Deep Singh is the old man who finished his.
screen: `BABA — ELDER, GRANDFATHER.` · `THE SCHOLAR WHO COPIED THE GRANTH.` · `1757: A VOW TO FREE THE HARMANDIR.` · `THE ACCOUNTS DIFFER; THE VOW HELD.` · then, large: `FINISH THE VOW.`

segments.voice: Think of something you started and left undone. A book half read. A message half written. A promise to call someone. A project in a drawer. Pick one that still matters. Picture it finished: what it looks like, what it feels like. Now decide the very next step, small enough to do today. Not the whole thing, just the next step. Let that decision settle in your body. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Baba. Elder, grandfather, a title of love — given to the old scholar-warrior who vowed to free the Harmandir in 1757 and, tradition says, fought on until he reached it.
Your line: finish the vow. Today, take the next step on one thing you started and left undone. Day two hundred ninety.

291.title: The great holocaust, 1762
291.hook: Ahmad Shah Abdali's army kills a great many Sikhs in a day, then blows up the Harmandir
291.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Vadda Ghallughara each year, especially near Kup-Rahira, where a memorial and gurdwara stand; the rebuilding of the Harmandir after 1764 is remembered as the panth rising again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baba, and your line, finish the vow. Did one unfinished thing get its next step? Today is the second of those two years Sikhs remember carefully. Day two hundred ninety-one.

A winter morning in February, 1762, on the flat farmland southwest of Ludhiana. A long, slow column is moving across the fields. Not an army, mostly. Families. Grandparents on carts, children on their mothers' hips, cooking pots, cattle, everything they own. They're heading for safety in the dry country to the south. The fighters ride alongside. And then, on the horizon, dust. An army that had marched through the night. Today: Vadda Ghallughara, the great holocaust.
screen: `FEBRUARY, 1762.` → `A COLUMN OF FAMILIES.` → `DUST ON THE HORIZON.`

segments.voice: Vadda means great, large. Ghallughara, as we heard a few days ago, means a massacre, a great destruction. The army belonged to Ahmad Shah Abdali, the king of Afghanistan, who invaded northern India many times. He had marched fast to catch the Sikhs off guard, near the village of Kup. The Sikh fighters did something remarkable. They formed a moving ring around the families, and kept the whole column walking, fighting on the outside while the old and the young moved in the middle. They kept moving through the whole day. But the losses were terrible. Many thousands were killed in that one day, among them many women, children and old people. The old accounts give numbers from about ten thousand to far more. Nobody knows exactly. That spring, at Vaisakhi, Abdali came to Amritsar. His men packed the Harmandir with gunpowder and blew it up, and filled the sacred pool with rubble. It looked like the end. It wasn't. That same autumn, the Sikhs gathered at Amritsar at Diwali and faced Abdali's army again, and he withdrew. Within two years they were rebuilding the Harmandir, and clearing the pool, brick by brick. Soon after, the Sikhs held Lahore. That's why the Sikh memory of 1762 has two halves. One is grief, held carefully and without hatred for anyone living today. The other is the comeback, told with quiet pride: the panth rose again.
screen: `VADDA — GREAT.` · `KUP, 1762: A MOVING RING OF FIGHTERS.` · `THE HARMANDIR BLOWN UP.` · `REBUILT BRICK BY BRICK.` · then, large: `THE PANTH ROSE AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Breathe slowly now. On each in-breath, let yourself remember: the families in the column, and anyone you know who has lived through loss. On each out-breath, let a little of the weight go, not the memory, just the weight. Slow in, remembering. Slow out, releasing. If you pray, you can hold them in the prayer you know. Keep the rhythm going on its own. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Vadda Ghallughara. The great holocaust of 1762, when many thousands of Sikhs were killed in a single day and the Harmandir was destroyed. And the panth rose again.
Your line: the panth rose again. Today, notice one person or place that came back from something hard, and honor it. Day two hundred ninety-one.

292.title: The Misls
292.hook: twelve Sikh confederacies rule parts of Punjab in the late 1700s
292.howItsDone: Some Sikh families still trace their history to one of the twelve misls; the misl period is taught in Sikh history as the bridge between the persecution of the early 1700s and the kingdom of Maharaja Ranjit Singh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vadda Ghallughara, and your line, the panth rose again. Did you honor something that came back from hard times? Today, what the panth rose into. Day two hundred ninety-two.

A big extended family can work like a small federation. Every household runs its own home, its own budget, its own arguments. Cousins compete. Uncles don't always speak. But when there's a wedding, or a funeral, or someone's in trouble, everyone shows up, and for a day they're one family. In the late 1700s, Punjab was run a little like that. After decades of being hunted, the Sikhs now held the land, not as one kingdom, but as twelve. Today: the misls.
screen: `MANY HOUSEHOLDS, ONE FAMILY.` → `EVERYONE SHOWS UP.` → `PUNJAB IN THE 1700S: TWELVE.`

segments.voice: A misl was a Sikh confederacy: a band of fighters and their families under a leader, a sardar, holding its own territory. By the second half of the 1700s, as Afghan and Mughal power in Punjab faded, there were twelve main misls. They had names, some from a leader's village, some from a trait. The Bhangis, who at one time held Lahore and Amritsar. The Ahluwalias, led by Jassa Singh, the commander we met with the Dal Khalsa. The Ramgarhias, the Kanhaiyas, the Sukerchakias, and others. Each ran its own affairs. And they did not always get along. Misls competed, feuded, and sometimes fought each other. Historians don't hide that. Where the word misl comes from, sources differ. It's an Arabic word. Some explain it as alike or equal, because the misls were meant to be equals. Others as a file or record, because the bands were listed in one register. Both fit. Here's the part that makes the misls more than a set of rival chiefdoms. Twice a year, at Vaisakhi and Diwali, they still came to Amritsar as the Sarbat Khalsa, sat before the Guru Granth Sahib, and could pass a gurmata together. Faced with an outside threat, the twelve could move as one Dal Khalsa. Many also offered rakhi, protection, to villages in return for a share of the harvest. It was untidy, and it lasted only a few decades. But it held the Sikhs together through a dangerous time, and one of those twelve would soon produce a young leader who'd unite most of them.
screen: `MISL — A SIKH CONFEDERACY.` · `TWELVE, EACH WITH ITS OWN SARDAR.` · `RIVALS, WHO SOMETIMES FEUDED.` · `ONE BEFORE THE GURU, TWICE A YEAR.` · then, large: `TWELVE, AND ONE.`

segments.voice: Think of a group you belong to: your family, a team, friends, a congregation, a class. Picture the people in it, all different, some of whom don't quite get along. Now ask: what holds us together anyway? A shared meal, a shared story, something we all care about more than our quarrels? Name that one thing. Notice it, and let yourself be grateful for it. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Misl. One of the twelve Sikh confederacies that ruled parts of Punjab in the late 1700s: separate, often rival, and one before the Guru.
Your line: twelve, and one. Today, in a group that argues, point once to the thing you all share. Day two hundred ninety-two.

293.title: Maharaja Ranjit Singh
293.hook: he unites Punjab in 1799 and covers the Harmandir in gold, giving it the name the world knows
293.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh as the ruler of the Sikh Empire; his samadhi stands in Lahore, and the gilding he gave to Harmandir Sahib, which Sikhs often call Darbar Sahib, is renewed and cared for to this day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the misl, twelve Sikh confederacies. Your line was twelve, and one. Today, the young leader from one of those twelve who made them one kingdom. Day two hundred ninety-three.

A shining building sits in the middle of a still pool, its upper walls and dome glowing gold, reflected upside down in the water. Pilgrims walk around it barefoot, day and night. Photos of it hang on kitchen walls and glow on phone screens around the world. But it didn't always look like that. For generations it stood in brick and stone. The gold came later, from a king. Today: Maharaja Ranjit Singh.
screen: `A SHINING BUILDING IN A STILL POOL.` → `ON WALLS AND PHONES WORLDWIDE.` → `THE GOLD CAME LATER.`

segments.voice: Ranjit Singh was born in 1780, the son of the leader of the Sukerchakia misl. As a small child he survived smallpox, which left him blind in one eye. He became chief as a boy, and in 1799, still a young man, he rode into Lahore and took the city. Over the next years he brought the misls and much of the land around them under one rule. In 1801 he was proclaimed Maharaja, great king, of Punjab. He ruled for almost forty years, until his death in 1839. His was a Sikh kingdom, but not only for Sikhs. Muslims and Hindus served at the top of his government; his foreign minister was a Muslim scholar. Then there's the gold. Ranjit Singh gave generously to many places of worship, and above all to the Harmandir in Amritsar, the temple the Afghans had destroyed and the Sikhs had rebuilt. Over years of work, its upper stories were covered in gilded copper, and inlaid marble was added below. English-speaking visitors called it the Golden Temple, and the name stuck. Sikhs usually call it Harmandir Sahib, the house of God, or Darbar Sahib, the Guru's court. There's a story Sikhs love to tell about him. When the Maharaja was once accused of breaking the Sikh code, he was summoned before the Akal Takht and he went, bowed, and accepted its judgment, like any other Sikh. Remember the two flags at the Akal Takht, the flag of the spirit standing a little higher? That day, the king took his place beneath it.
screen: `SUKERCHAKIA MISL, BORN 1780.` · `LAHORE 1799, MAHARAJA 1801.` · `GOLD FOR THE HARMANDIR.` · `A KING WHO BOWED TO THE AKAL TAKHT.` · then, large: `THE GOLDEN TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: Look around you and pick something plain. A mug, a chair, a window, your own hands. Look at it the way pilgrims look at the Golden Temple: slowly, as if it were precious. Where did it come from? Who made it? What has it done for you? Let it shine a little in your attention, without changing anything about it. That's the gold you can add to anything. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Maharaja. Great king — the title taken by Ranjit Singh in 1801, the Sikh king who united Punjab, covered the Harmandir in gold, and still bowed to the Akal Takht.
Your line: the golden temple. Today, look at one plain thing as if it were gold. Day two hundred ninety-three.

294.title: Annexation, 1849
294.hook: after two wars with the British, Punjab is annexed and the boy king Duleep Singh sent to England
294.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the annexation of 1849 as the end of the Sikh kingdom; Maharaja Duleep Singh's story is widely told in the Sikh diaspora, especially in Britain, where a statue of him stands in Thetford, Norfolk.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maharaja, and your line, the golden temple. Did something plain shine for a moment? Today, what happened to his kingdom, and to his youngest son. Then a look back at the week. Day two hundred ninety-four.

A ten-year-old boy sits on a throne too big for him. He's the king, officially. His mother has been taken away from him. Grown men decide his future over his head. And one spring day in 1849, he's asked to sign a paper that gives away his kingdom, and a diamond famous across the world. A few years later, he'll be living in England, thousands of miles from Punjab. Today: annexation, and the boy king Duleep Singh.

segments.voice: After Ranjit Singh died in 1839, his kingdom fell into a decade of turmoil: rulers came and went, and several were killed. The British East India Company, already ruling much of India, was watching. Two wars followed between the Sikh kingdom and the British, in 1845 and 1848. The Sikh armies fought hard, and some battles cost the British dearly. But the kingdom lost. In March 1849, Punjab was annexed, taken into British India. The last Maharaja, Duleep Singh, Ranjit Singh's youngest son, was about ten. He was separated from his mother, Maharani Jind Kaur, placed with a British guardian, and the Koh-i-Noor diamond was sent to Queen Victoria. As a young teenager he became a Christian, and at fifteen he was taken to England, where he lived the life of a country gentleman. As a young man he was allowed to bring his mother to England, and she lived near him until her death. Years later, in his forties, he tried to return to Punjab and took up his Sikh faith once more. He was stopped on the way, and he died in Paris in 1893, far from home. Sikhs remember him with a particular ache, as the king who lost his home, his mother and his kingdom as a child. Now the week. The Chhota Ghallughara: remembered. Gurmata: decide together. Baba Deep Singh: finish the vow. The Vadda Ghallughara: the panth rose again. The misls: twelve, and one. Ranjit Singh: the golden temple. And annexation: far from home.

A friend who moved abroad, a grandparent who left their village long ago, a student in a new city, a soldier, a refugee you've read about. Picture them where they are this evening.
